title: Can a Language Model Write the Weights? An Empirical Study of LLM-Written Scoring Networks for Column Generation and MILP Branching, with a Bus-Driver Scheduling Application
read_level: full (v1 PDF, 17 pages incl. appendices A-C)
why_wsp: An LLM (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) writes the weights of small MLP scoring networks (JSON, each weight justified) for column generation and SCIP branching, reading forward-pass diagnostics and editing by hand with no gradient fitting.
domain: operations research: VRPTW column generation, MILP branching in SCIP, bus-driver crew scheduling (MARTA GTFS)
editor: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), as an agent in Claude Code
target: small MLPs stored as JSON; "most networks in this paper have one linear layer or one ReLU layer of width 6"; branching rule v1 is a 6-term closed-form score over 7 features
interface: direct values (JSON weight file with free-text note per weight)
loop: closed-loop with feedback (LLM reads practice-set diagnostics such as strong-branching agreement and tree size, edits v0 to v1; frozen before test)
self_editing: no; the LLM writes separate small scoring networks (paper notes the same model also wrote the paper)

headline_results.quote: the LLM-written arc scorer ties the classical reduced-cost rule (time ratio 1.02 over 34 instances
v1 is faster on all 18 instances, with a geometric-mean time ratio of 0.37 (p = 7.6 × 10−6 )

headline_results.claim: Set cover ties with larger trees
headline_results.quote: On set cover it ties on time (0.90, p = 0.14) with 1.3–1.4× larger trees.

headline_results.claim: Hand-written vs trained weights on same features
headline_results.quote: hand-written weights match or beat weights trained by imitation of strong branching in 3 of 4 settings
v1 solves 19 instances against 24 for the default

headline_results.claim: MARTA gain fully matched by SCIP pseudocost rule
headline_results.quote: it is as fast as the LLM-written rules (vm_fast/pscost time ratio 0.99, p = 0.19)
The lookahead variant did not generalise (1.05×, p = 0.51, 22 solved).

cost.claim: Compute environment and duration only; no token or $ cost
cost.quote: Apple M5, 10 cores, 32 GB RAM, macOS 27) between 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-05

baselines_and_controls: SCIP default (reliability pseudocost), full strong branching, SCIP plain pseudocost, most-infeasible, random pick; same-architecture networks trained by imitation of strong branching (7 inputs, 16 ReLU, 2,166 nodes); classical reduced-cost top-K arc rule and cheapest-label eviction in column generation.
runs_and_variance: Paired runs on held-out instance sets (18 IS, 10+8 SC, 39 MIPLIB, 32 MARTA); paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on log time ratios; shifted geometric means. Fixed SCIP seed; no multi-seed variance reported.
robustness_of_edits: Distribution shift tested: synthetic-family rule "was not general: on 39 MIPLIB 2017 instances it solved 19 versus 24" (Abstract); lookahead tuned on 8 practice instances overfit.
verification: none on weights; exactness guaranteed by host solver ("The algorithms stay exact whatever the weights are"); statistical tests (Wilcoxon).
memorization_vs_reasoning: Each weight has a written justification (e.g. pseudocost weight "cut from 0.7 to 0.2 because the disagreements came from candidates with high but noisy early pseudocosts", Sec. 5); authors conclude "the gains came from being cheap, not from what the LLM wrote" (Abstract).
limitations_stated: Concurrent runs vary time across batches; features in Python for Studies 2-3; two SCIP versions; small instance sets (8-40); synthetic MARTA labour rules and garage grouping; small trained baseline; "The same AI wrote the weights, ran the analysis and wrote this paper" (Sec. 8).
cites_or_builds_on: Takehi et al. 2026, Sparks of Weight-Space Programming (blog)
notes_for_survey: Paper text, code, design and all network weights were generated by Claude Opus 5.5 under author direction (disclosed). Includes a strong cheap-baseline control (SCIP pseudocost) that fully explains the applied speedup; the only attributable gain is on synthetic independent set. Useful negative/controlled-evaluation data point for WSP in OR.
